previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of cocaine-induced cardiomyopathy, systolic heart failure, COPD, and chronic kidney disease was admitted for recurrent syncope associated with coughing. He presented with worsening dyspnea, weight gain to 91 kg, and signs of fluid overload. Workup revealed elevated BNP and mild pulmonary edema on imaging, consistent with acute on chronic heart failure. His syncope was evaluated with normal head CT, EKG, and telemetry; neurology attributed the episodes to cough-induced syncope. He was treated with IV diuresis, achieving a discharge weight of 84.7 kg, with improvement in symptoms and renal function (creatinine from 2.4 to 1.6). Losartan was uptitrated to 25 mg daily, and plans were made for outpatient follow-up with cardiology, pulmonology for a suspicious right upper lobe nodule, and primary care for iron deficiency anemia. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions on weight monitoring, medication adherence, and low-salt diet.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ year old male with a past medical history of 
systolic CHF (non ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy [EF ___ 
felt to be from cocaine abuse), CKD, prior DVT, IDDM who 
presented to the ___ ED with recurrent syncopal episodes in 
the setting of coughing.

ACTIVE ISSUES:  
# Syncope: Recurrent and associated with deep coughing episodes. 
Given the direct association with these episodes and his known 
cardiopulmonary disease, concern that he has transiently reduced 
cerebral perfusion due to decreased preload when he increases 
his intrathoracic pressure. No clinical evidence of seizures 
outside of some urinary incontinence when he syncopizes, though 
he immediately regains consciousness without post-ictal state. 
Per ENT evaluation, there was no vocal cord dysfunction on 
nasopharyngoscopy. Per pulmonary consult, we optimized 
medications for his GERD (increased PPI dose and added 
ranitidine), COPD (started azithromycin course), as well as 
symptomatic treatment with benzonatate and increased dose of 
gabapentin. Patient reported significantly improved cough by day 
of discharge and had no syncopal or pre-syncopal episodes during 
this admission.

# Acute on chronic systolic CHF: Hemodynamically stable, 
evidenced by worsening of orthopnea, PND, and significant JVP 
elevation on exam. BNP within recent baseline but clinically he 
appeared overloaded at admission. LVEF ___ on most recent 
___ TTE, NYHA III-IV. He was diuresed with IV furosemide and 
discharge weight was 82.4kg, close to his known dry weight of 
~82kg.

# r/o ACS: Chest pain with elevated troponin at admission, 
however the nature of his chest pain is more consistent with 
musculoskeletal etiology given its reproducibility and 
association with coughing. His troponin elevation is favored to 
be due to demand in the setting of acute on chronic severe 
systolic CHF, though was stable on recheck. Chest-pain free 
during admission.   

CHRONIC ISSUES:  
# T2DM: Continued on home glargine and insulin sliding scale.  
# COPD: PFTs ___ with FEV1 68%, FEV1/FVC 97%. At baseline, 
patient on 2L home O2. Started on azithromycin for 5-day course.

# HLD: Continued home pravastatin.  
# HTN: Continued home losartan.  
# Gout: Continued home colchicine.  
# Anxiety/Insomnia: Continued on home diphenhydramine, 
lorazepam, and traodone.  
# GERD: Continued on home omeprazole.  
# Chronic pain: Continued on home tramadol and gabapentin 
(increased for chronic cough).
